title: Random Variables 3B: Normal Probabilities and Applications

topics.title: Finding 𝝁 or 𝝈 given a Probability

inlines.text: solves problems involving discrete probability distributions, continuous random variables and the normal distribution
Identify the normal distribution as a continuous probability distribution that is used to model many naturally occurring phenomena

Identify the graph of the probability density function of a normal distribution, the normal curve, as an ‘ideal’ bell-shaped curve, symmetrical about its mean which is equal to its mode and median, and as having most values concentrated about the mean
Identify contexts that can be approximately modelled by a normal random variable
to represent a normally distributed random variable that has mean
Represent probabilities associated with the normal distribution by areas of shaded regions under the normal curve, which may extend to

Apply the empirical rule to make judgements and solve problems involving probabilities of normally distributed data: that for normal distributions, approximately 68% of data lie within one standard deviation of the mean, approximately 95% within two standard deviations of the mean and approximately 99.7% within three standard deviations of the mean
Use graphing applications to explore the normal distribution, graph the probability density function
, verify the empirical rule and graph the cumulative distribution function
Recognise features of the normal curve, and identify the global maximum and points of inflection
Distinguish between a standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and the non-standard normal distribution with mean
Define the z-score, or standardised score, by the formula
is an observed value of a random variable
Interpret the z-score as the number of standard deviations a score lies above or below the mean
Use z-scores to compare scores from different sets of data and justify conclusions
Use z-scores to identify probabilities of events less or more extreme than a given outcome and solve problems using tables for the standard normal distribution
Solve problems involving finding the mean or standard deviation of a normal random variable given the probability of an event less or more extreme than a given outcome
Use z-scores to make judgements related to probabilities of certain events or given sets of data assuming an underlying normal distribution

content.prompt: The lifetimes of a brand of light bulb are normally distributed with mean 1200 hours and SD 80 hours. Find $P(X < 960\text{ hours})$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\frac{960-1200}{80}\\&=-3\end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule, approximately $99.7\%$ of values lie within three standard deviations of the mean. The remaining probability is split equally between the two tails.
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<960)&=P(z<-3)\\&\approx\frac{1-0.997}{2}\\&=0.0015\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt:
A study found mean cholesterol level 219 mg/mL with standard deviation 41 mg/mL for adult males without heart disease. Assume cholesterol levels in this population are normally distributed.

Doctors classify a reading above 240 mg/mL as high.

What percentage of this population has high cholesterol? Use the standard normal table and give your answer to the nearest whole percent.

answer.worked:
Let $X$ be the cholesterol level in mg/mL.

$$\begin{aligned}z&=\frac{240-219}{41}\\z&=\frac{21}{41}\\z&\approx0.51\end{aligned}$$

From the standard normal table, $P(Z\le0.51)=0.6950$.

$$\begin{aligned}P(X>240)&\approx P(Z>0.51)\\P(X>240)&\approx1-0.6950\\P(X>240)&\approx0.3050\end{aligned}$$

The percentage is approximately $0.3050\times100\%=30.50\%$, or $31\%$ to the nearest whole percent.

content.prompt: The weights of 10 000 newborn babies in NSW are normally distributed. These weights have a mean of 3.1 kg and a standard deviation of 0.35 kg.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What is the probability that a randomly chosen baby has a weight between 3.24 kg and 3.66 kg? Use the standard normal table and give your answer correct to 4 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Let $X$ be a baby's weight in kilograms.
$$\begin{aligned}z_{\text{lower}}&=\frac{3.24-3.1}{0.35}\\z_{\text{lower}}&=0.4\\z_{\text{upper}}&=\frac{3.66-3.1}{0.35}\\z_{\text{upper}}&=1.6\end{aligned}$$
Using the standard normal table,
$$\begin{aligned}P(3.24<X<3.66)&=P(0.4<Z<1.6)\\P(3.24<X<3.66)&=P(Z\le1.6)-P(Z\le0.4)\\P(3.24<X<3.66)&\approx0.9452-0.6554\\P(3.24<X<3.66)&\approx0.2898.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many of the 10 000 newborn babies would have a weight between 3.24 kg and 3.66 kg?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Expected number}&=10\,000\times0.2898\\\text{Expected number}&=2898.\end{aligned}$$
Approximately 2898 babies would have a weight between 3.24 kg and 3.66 kg.

content.prompt: Packets of sugar are filled and labelled as having a weight of 1 kg. The weights of these packets are normally distributed with a mean of 1.01 kg and a standard deviation of 0.01 kg. A packet of sugar is rejected if its weight is lower than 985 g.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What is the probability that a randomly chosen packet of sugar is rejected? Give your answer correct to 4 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Let $X$ be the packet weight in kilograms. The rejection threshold is $985\text{ g}=0.985\text{ kg}$.
$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{0.985-1.01}{0.01}\\z&=-2.5\end{align*}$$
By symmetry and the standard normal table,
$$\begin{align*}P(X<0.985)&=P(Z<-2.5)\\P(X<0.985)&=1-P(Z\le2.5)\\P(X<0.985)&\approx1-0.9938\\P(X<0.985)&\approx0.0062.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: From a batch of 1000 packets of sugar, how many packets would you expect to be rejected?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Expected number rejected}&=np\\\text{Expected number rejected}&\approx1000\times0.0062\\\text{Expected number rejected}&\approx6.2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\mu-3\sigma&=28-3(0.833)\\&=25.501\\\mu+3\sigma&=28+3(0.833)\\&=30.499\end{align*}$$
The expected range is approximately $25.5$ cm to $30.5$ cm, containing about $99.7\%$ of heights under the normal model.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What percentage of dogs are between $27.2$ and $30$ cm tall?

answer.worked:
Let $X$ be a dog's height in centimetres. The endpoint z-scores are
$$\begin{align*}z_{27.2}&=\frac{27.2-28}{0.833}\\&\approx-0.96\\z_{30}&=\frac{30-28}{0.833}\\&\approx2.40\end{align*}$$
Using symmetry and the standard normal table,
$$\begin{align*}P(27.2\le X\le30)&\approx P(-0.96\le Z\le2.40)\\&=P(Z\le2.40)-P(Z\le-0.96)\\&=0.9918-(1-0.8315)\\&=0.8233.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Loaf masses from a bakery are normally distributed with a mean of 750 g and standard deviation of 12 g. A loaf is unusual if the probability of a loaf being at least as far from the mean, in either direction, is less than 0.05. Is a 730 g loaf unusual? Use the standard normal distribution table. Round calculated z-scores to 2 decimal places and give probabilities to 4 decimal places.

answer.short: No. The probability is $0.0950$, which is not less than $0.05$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\frac{730-750}{12}\\z&=-\frac53\\z&\approx-1.67\end{aligned}$$
By symmetry,
$$\begin{aligned}P(Z\le-1.67)&=1-P(Z\le1.67)\\&=1-0.9525\\&=0.0475\end{aligned}$$
Both directions count, so
$$\begin{aligned}P(|Z|\ge1.67)&=2\times0.0475\\&=0.0950\end{aligned}$$
Since $0.0950>0.05$, a 730 g loaf is not unusual.

content.prompt: A machine fills cereal boxes with weights that are normally distributed with mean 500 g and standard deviation 2 g. To ensure boxes are above the advertised weight at least 95% of the time, what is the greatest whole-gram weight that should be printed on the box?

answer.worked:
Let $w$ be the advertised weight. We require $P(X>w)\geq0.95$, so $P(X\leq w)\leq0.05$.

From the table, $P(Z\leq1.6)=0.9452$ and $P(Z\leq1.7)=0.9554$. Using the midpoint estimate and symmetry gives $z\approx-1.65$ for the lower 5% cutoff.

$$\begin{aligned}w&\approx500+(-1.65)(2)\\w&\approx496.7\text{ g}\end{aligned}$$

The greatest whole-gram advertised weight below this cutoff is **496 g**. Checking this choice:

$$\begin{aligned}z&=\frac{496-500}{2}\\z&=-2\\P(X>496)&=P(Z<2)\\P(X>496)&=0.9772\end{aligned}$$

Thus about 97.72% of boxes exceed the advertised weight, satisfying the requirement.

answer.worked:
We want $P(Z<z)=0.70$. From the table, $P(Z\le0.5)=0.6915$ and $P(Z\le0.6)=0.7257$. Since $0.70$ is about a quarter of the way from $0.6915$ to $0.7257$, $z\approx0.525$.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\mu+z\sigma\\x&\approx162+0.525(6.5)\\x&\approx165.4\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$Round up to give a minimum whole-centimetre height of $166\text{ cm}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Men's heights have mean 178 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. A bed is made long enough that only 1% of men are taller than it. Find the minimum bed length, in whole centimetres.

answer.worked:
$P(X\le x)=1-0.01=0.99$, so we want $P(Z<z)=0.99$. From the table, $P(Z\le2.3)=0.9893$ and $P(Z\le2.4)=0.9918$. Since $0.99$ is about $0.28$ of the way from $0.9893$ to $0.9918$, $z\approx2.33$.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\mu+z\sigma\\x&\approx178+2.33(8)\\x&\approx196.6\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$Round up to give a minimum whole-centimetre length of $197\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt:
The graph shows a normal distribution.

Approximately $99.7\%$ of the area under the curve is bounded by $x=25$ and $x=145$.

Which of the following gives the correct mean and variance of the distribution?
(A) mean = $60$ and variance = $20$
(B) mean = $60$ and variance = $400$
(C) mean = $85$ and variance = $20$
(D) mean = $85$ and variance = $400$

answer.worked:
Approximately $99.7\%$ of a normal distribution lies within $3$ standard deviations of the mean.
$$\begin{align*}\mu&=\frac{25+145}{2}\\&=85\end{align*}$$
The distance from the mean to either bound is $60$.
$$\begin{align*}3\sigma&=60\\\sigma&=20\\\sigma^2&=400\end{align*}$$
Correct answer: (D).

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Assume that the probability density function of a normal random variable with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ is
$$f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}.$$
Use the trapezoidal rule with FOUR sub-intervals to estimate $P(49<X<77)$ correct to four decimal places.
Interpret your conclusions with reference to the empirical rule.

answer.worked:
For $X$, use $\mu=70$ and $\sigma=7$. Thus:
$$\begin{align*}
P(49<X<77)&=\int_{49}^{77}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi(7^2)}}e^{-\frac{(x-70)^2}{2(7^2)}}\,dx \\
&=\int_{49}^{77}\frac{1}{7\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x-70)^2}{98}}\,dx
\end{align*}$$
Using four sub-intervals gives step size:
$$\begin{align*}
h&=\frac{77-49}{4} \\
&=7
\end{align*}$$
The required $x$-values are $49,56,63,70,77$. The trapezoidal approximation is:
$$\begin{align*}
P(49<X<77)&\approx\frac{7}{2}\left[f(49)+2f(56)+2f(63)+2f(70)+f(77)\right] \\
&=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\left(e^{-\frac{9}{2}}+2e^{-2}+2e^{-\frac{1}{2}}+2+e^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) \\
&\approx0.8181
\end{align*}$$
This interval corresponds to $-3<Z<1$. By the empirical rule, the approximate probability is:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{99.7\%}{2}+\frac{68\%}{2}&=83.85\%
\end{align*}$$
The trapezoidal estimate is reasonably consistent with this, allowing for the use of only four sub-intervals.

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Let $Y$ be the English Advanced mark of a randomly chosen student, prior to rounding.
Suppose that $Y$ can be modelled by a normal distribution in a similar way to $X$.
The probability density functions of $X$ and $Y$ were plotted on the same set of axes.
A student recorded the $x$-coordinate of each function's local maximum.
Which one of the random variables had the lesser value for the local maximum of its probability density function?

answer.worked: The local maximum of a normal probability density function occurs at its mean. Since the English Advanced mean is $57$ and the Mathematics Advanced mean is $70$, the random variable with the lesser $x$-coordinate for the local maximum is $Y$.

children.label: d

Relative to their cohort, which subject did the student perform better in?

answer.worked:
Compare the two $z$-scores.
$$\begin{align*}
z_{\text{English}}&=\frac{76-57}{17} \\
&\approx1.1176 \\
z_{\text{Mathematics}}&=\frac{76-70}{7} \\
&\approx0.8571
\end{align*}$$
The student performed better relative to the English Advanced cohort because the English Advanced $z$-score is larger.

children.label: e
children.prompt:
Another student attained the same mark for both English Advanced and Mathematics Advanced.
She performed equally well relative to both cohorts.
What mark has the student attained for both subjects?

answer.worked:
Let the common mark be $x$. Equal relative performance means the two $z$-scores are equal.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{x-57}{17}&=\frac{x-70}{7} \\
7(x-57)&=17(x-70) \\
7x-399&=17x-1190 \\
791&=10x \\
x&=79.1
\end{align*}$$
The student attained a mark of $79.1$ in both subjects.

flags.note:
[Pedagogy audit v2 · Applied automatically · New teaching] The lesson never states that P(a≤X≤b) equals the integral of the density from a to b. Questions 1 and 2 use integral estimates as probabilities, so add this link after the density formula.
Worked example: Let $X$ be normally distributed with mean 50 and SD 6, with density $f(x)$. Numerical integration gives $\displaystyle\int_{44}^{56}f(x)\,dx\approx0.6827$. Find $P(X\ge56)$ to 3 decimal places.
The probability is the area under the density between the limits.
$$P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$$
$$P(44\le X\le56)=\int_{44}^{56}f(x)\,dx\approx0.6827$$
The total area is 1 and the curve is symmetric about 50, so the two tails are equal.
$$\begin{align*}P(X\ge56)&\approx\frac{1-0.6827}{2}\\&=0.15865\\&\approx0.159\end{align*}$$
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Numerical integration gives each integral below. Use it to find the probability.
a) $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}\phi(z)\,dz\approx0.9545$. Find $P(-2\le Z\le2)$.

c) $X$ has mean 50 and SD 6, with density $f(x)$, and $\displaystyle\int_{44}^{62}f(x)\,dx\approx0.8186$. Find the probability that $X$ lies outside the interval from 44 to 62, to 3 decimal places.
Answers: a) $0.9545$; b) $0.023$; c) $0.181$

entries.description:
Ordered syllabus bullet list:
1. Identify the normal distribution as a continuous probability distribution that is used to model many naturally occurring phenomena
2. Identify the graph of the probability density function of a normal distribution, the normal curve, as an ‘ideal’ bell-shaped curve, symmetrical about its mean which is equal to its mode and median, and as having most values concentrated about the mean
3. Identify contexts that can be approximately modelled by a normal random variable
4. Use the notation X ∼ N(μ, σ²) to represent a normally distributed random variable that has mean μ and standard deviation σ
5. Represent probabilities associated with the normal distribution by areas of shaded regions under the normal curve, which may extend to ±∞
6. Apply the empirical rule to make judgements and solve problems involving probabilities of normally distributed data: that for normal distributions, approximately 68% of data lie within one standard deviation of the mean, approximately 95% within two standard deviations of the mean and approximately 99.7% within three standard deviations of the mean
7. Use graphing applications to explore the normal distribution, graph the probability density function f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))]e^{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}, verify the empirical rule and graph the cumulative distribution function
8. Recognise features of the normal curve, and identify the global maximum and points of inflection
9. Distinguish between a standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and the non-standard normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ
10. Define the z-score, or standardised score, by the formula z = (x−μ)/σ, where μ is the mean and σ is the standard deviation, and x is an observed value of a random variable
11. Interpret the z-score as the number of standard deviations a score lies above or below the mean
12. Use z-scores to compare scores from different sets of data and justify conclusions
13. Use z-scores to identify probabilities of events less or more extreme than a given outcome and solve problems using tables for the standard normal distribution
14. Solve problems involving finding the mean or standard deviation of a normal random variable given the probability of an event less or more extreme than a given outcome
15. Use z-scores to make judgements related to probabilities of certain events or given sets of data assuming an underlying normal distribution

entries.description:
Finding the Equivalent Score
For a score in dataset A, to find the equivalent score in dataset B:
1. Calculate z-score of the raw score in dataset A. z_A = (x_A − μ_A)/σ_A
2. Calculate the raw score in dataset B using dataset A’s z-score. x_B = μ_B + z_Aσ_B

presentation.heading: Example
presentation.subtitle: Find the equivalent score using the z-score
presentation.workingLayout: Two columns separated by a thin vertical rule; calculate the mathematics z-score on the left, then the equivalent English score on the right.

entries.description:
Left column:
1. Calculate z-score for maths
z_M = (x_M − μ_M)/σ_M
z_M = (64 − 59)/9
     = 0.56

Right column:
2. Calculate equivalent score in English using maths z-score
x_E = μ_E + z_Mσ_E
     = 50 + 0.56(6)
     = 53.36

entries.description:
We want P(Z ≤ z) = 0.001
This would be a negative z-score, so
P(Z ≤ −z) = P(Z ≥ z)
             = 1 − P(Z ≤ z)
             = 1 − 0.001
             = 0.999
Using the table, P(Z ≤ 3.1) = 0.999
So z = −3.1:
−3.1 = (100 − μ)/2
−6.2 = 100 − μ
μ = 106.2 g

entries.description: PDF for Standard Normal Curve

For any normal curve with μ and σ:
 f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] · e^{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}

For the standard normal curve μ = 0, σ = 1:
 φ(z) = [1/√(2π)]e^{−(1/2)z²}
Notice that every normal curve is a transformation of the standard curve f(x) = φ((x−μ)/σ)

entries.description:
The standard curve φ(z) has these properties:
• Total area under the curve is 1.
• Even symmetry.
• Mean, median, mode (global max) at z = 0.
• y-intercept at 1/√(2π) ≈ 0.4.
• y → 0 as z → ±∞
• Points of inflection are 1 SD from the mean.

entries.description: Explain why the percentage of scores between 46 and 70 is twice your answer to part (a)
entries.expectedAnswer: 46 and 70 are equally distant from the mean 58 on opposite sides. Symmetry gives equal probabilities between 46 and 58 and between 58 and 70, so the combined percentage is double.

presentation.responseSpace: Open explanation space beneath the prompt.

entries.description:
Supplied blue explanation:
46 = 58 − 12 and 70 = 58 + 12: both are the same distance from the mean on opposite sides.
By symmetry of the normal distribution, P(46 < x < 58) = P(58 < x < 70),
so the percentage between 46 and 70 is double.

entries.description:
